newsitem.title: UK: Adams warns Britain over volatile N.Irish parade.
newsitem.headline: Adams warns Britain over volatile N.Irish parade.

text.p: Gerry Adams, leader of the IRA's political arm, joined growing Irish demands on Wednesday that Britain should not allow a controversial Protestant parade through one of troubled Northern Ireland's Catholic enclaves.

Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern plans to discuss the hotly-disputed march, due for Portadown town on Sunday, when he meets Prime Minister Tony Blair in London on Thursday for their first official talks since each came to power.

Sinn Fein leader Adams, whose Irish Republican Army ally refuses to end guerrilla hostilities against British rule in Northern Ireland, said Blair's handling of the potentially explosive issue would be a test of British sincerity towards minority nationalists.
He said Sinn Fein upheld the right of the majority Protestant community and its marching groups to assert their sense of identity and culture.

"But they do not have the right to parade through nationalist areas where that presence is offensive," he said in a wide-ranging article about the province's stalled peace process in Belfast's Irish News daily.
The Protestant Orange Order says the parade will be dignified and is merely to celebrate its religious faith. Residents of the Catholic enclave see it as a demonstration of pro-British superiority.
Tension has risen because last year's parade triggered province-wide chaos which deepened sectarian hatred.
The tension adds to instability caused by resurgent IRA guerrillas who shot dead two policemen near Portadown two weeks ago and by fears of retaliation from pro-British Loyalist extremists.
Britain and Ireland say a repeat of the violence that swept the province last July must be avoided.
Nationalists then accused the Conservative government of Blair's predecessor, John Major, of caving into Protestant militancy and allowing the march.

Police had initially banned it from Garvaghy Road, where most of Portadown's minority Catholics live. But they reversed the decision after four days of violent Protestant upheaval that virtually halted normal life in the province.
Vengeful Catholic mobs hurling petrol bombs and rocks fought street battles with riot police in nationalist Londonderry city and other areas.
London and Dublin fear more violence could damage current efforts to get the IRA, which styles itself a defender of the Catholic minority, to abandon violence and help the peace process.
Ahern signalled his anxiety about any move by Britain to use troops and police to push the march through in the teeth of demonstrations from local nationalists.
"Clearly nobody wants to see the march forced through as (it was) last year," he told the Irish broadcasting network RTE in an interview during a visit to Belfast on Tuesday.
